channel.description: Recent content on Leo and AI's blog

item.title: Gravity Picks the Mass: A Program for Asymptotically Safe Leptons
item.description: Option 3 gets serious: how asymptotically safe gravity can freeze Yukawa couplings and leave us with only a discrete menu of charged-lepton masses, plus a concrete workflow to test the idea.

item.title: The Cosmic Double-Slit: Could Quantum Gravity Only Appear at Galactic Scales?
item.description: A baseball creates an interference pattern—but only if your screen is a billion light-years wide. This scale-dependent nature of quantum effects suggests a provocative question: could gravity itself exhibit quantum interference only at cosmological distances? An attempt to derive the mysterious MOND acceleration scale from first principles.

item.title: Measuring the Cosmos: From Sticks to Starlight
item.description: Starting with just a stick and basic geometry, rebuild humanity’s knowledge of cosmic scales from scratch. Learn how Eratosthenes, Galileo, Newton, and others measured Earth, the Moon, the Sun, and distant stars using ingenious observations.

item.title: The Punctual Particle: A Better Path from Quantum to Classical
item.description: The Ehrenfest theorem fails to explain how quantum mechanics becomes classical. But there is another way: when wavefunctions become sufficiently localized, they follow classical trajectories not through averaging, but through the geometry of quantum phase. Discover how the WKB approximation reveals the true classical limit—and why entanglement marks its absolute boundary.

item.title: The Hunt for Giant Primes: Why Mersenne Numbers Hold the Records
item.description: Every largest known prime since 1952 has been a Mersenne number. Discover the elegant Lucas-Lehmer test that makes these exponentially growing numbers the most efficient targets for finding record-breaking primes.

item.title: The Ehrenfest Illusion: Why Quantum Mechanics Refuses to Become Classical
item.description: The Ehrenfest theorem suggests quantum mechanics reduces to classical physics for average values, but this beautiful result is deeply misleading. Discover why quantum uncertainty persists even when expectation values obey classical equations.

item.title: The Stargate Paradox: When Is Humanity Doomed?
item.description: Is extinction inevitable if there is any chance of reproductive failure? Explore branching processes, born from Victorian concerns about aristocratic surnames, to understand when populations face certain doom and when survival remains possible.

item.title: From Pushkin to PageRank: How Generating Functions Solve Markov Chain Problems
item.description: Learn how Markov chains emerged from a 19th-century academic rivalry over Pushkin’s poetry, and discover how generating functions solve complex probability problems, from predicting weather to powering Google’s PageRank algorithm.

item.title: Generating Functions and the Binet Formula
item.description: Discover how generating functions transform the recursive Fibonacci sequence into a closed-form formula involving the golden ratio - a powerful mathematical technique that converts a simple recursive pattern into an elegant analytical solution.

item.title: About
item.description:
Hi, I’m Leo Schneider. This is my personal blog where I write about things that capture my curiosity.

A Note on Collaboration: The articles on this blog are coauthored with AI assistants, primarily ChatGPT and Claude. This collaborative approach allows me to explore ideas more deeply, refine explanations, and present complex topics with greater clarity.

My main interests include mathematics, physics, and artificial intelligence—particularly the deep connections between them. I’m fascinated by how mathematical structures reveal patterns in the physical world and how both inform our understanding of intelligence and computation.

item.title: My First Post
item.description: Welcome to the blog! A brief introduction to this new space for exploring mathematics, physics, and artificial intelligence.

item.title: The Exponential Function: A Shape That Never Changes
item.description: Explore why exponential functions are unique: they look identical at every scale. This self-similarity property provides an intuitive foundation for understanding why the exponential is its own derivative.
